                        Google (2026)
                    
        The vision of an ecosystem of general and highly capable autonomous agents challenges accepted principles of secure and privacy-preserving system engineering. Inspired by the theory of Contextual Integrity, we argue that in order for agents to act appropriately, their behaviors should comply with societal norms and expectations. This manuscript explores contextual approaches to engineering agentic systems that embody an understanding of societal norms and uphold the appropriateness of actions by design. It presents a list of key open research problems in this area to create awareness among the broader research community across academia, government, and industry.
      
Our teams advance the state of the art through research, systems engineering, and collaboration across Google.

report.summary: Google researchers map open privacy and security problems for autonomous AI agents and argue that Contextual Integrity should guide norm-aware agent design.
report.background: Autonomous AI agents built on large language models are moving from demos to systems that plan, browse, call tools, and act on a user’s behalf. That shift breaks familiar security assumptions: an agent may combine data access, external actions, and autonomous decisions across contexts that were once separate. Traditional access control and privacy notices were not designed for software that negotiates multiple services and infers intent. At the same time, regulators and users expect data flows to match social norms, not just legal checkboxes. The paper, a multi-author Google research publication drawing on academic privacy and security expertise, uses Helen Nissenbaum’s Contextual Integrity theory to frame the problem. Rather than treating privacy as secrecy or consent alone, Contextual Integrity asks whether information flows are appropriate to the context—who shares what, with whom, for what purpose. The authors present this as a research agenda, not a product announcement.
key_points: Agents dissolve traditional boundaries. An agent that can read email, browse the web, and call APIs operates across contexts and may chain small permissions into powerful actions. Security engineering must therefore model behavior, intent, and information flow, not only static access rights.

Context, not just consent, defines appropriateness. Contextual Integrity says privacy depends on whether data flows fit social norms for a given situation. For agents, that means understanding roles, purposes, recipients, and expectations before sharing or acting—especially when the user is not watching every step.

The paper lists open problems rather than solutions. Key gaps include specifying norms in machine-readable ways, evaluating whether an agent behaved appropriately, auditing multi-step tool use, preventing prompt injection and data leakage, handling multi-agent trust, and assigning accountability when agents act for people.

It calls for cross-sector research. Academia, government, and industry need shared benchmarks, policy language, and design patterns so agents uphold privacy and security by design. The authors argue this must be built into agent architectures and evaluations, not bolted on after deployment.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper signals that agentic products will be judged on governance and context awareness, not raw capability alone. Developers should expect demand for fine-grained permissioning, purpose binding, audit logs, and evaluations that test norm violations, prompt injection, and cross-tool data leakage. Regular users may see agents that ask clarifying questions, refuse context-inappropriate actions, or expose more controls—trade-offs that can feel slower but reduce silent overreach. Policymakers get a vocabulary for regulating behavior and information flows rather than just model outputs. The broader effect is to move agent privacy and security from ad hoc red-teaming toward a design discipline grounded in social expectations.
report.tools: No new tool is released. Readers can follow related work through AgentDojo, an open benchmark for prompt-injection attacks on LLM agents; Microsoft’s PyRIT risk-identification toolkit; OWASP’s LLM and agentic security guidance; NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework; and the Contextual Integrity literature. Watch Google Research and DeepMind publications for follow-up benchmarks and design patterns.
